A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same d2 framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained content despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning-benchmark evaluations, likelihood-estimation diagnostics, toxicity-steering experiments, and ablations, including Table 2 and Figures 6–9.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds reasoning experiments on any-order causal LLaDA and a finetuning ablation, reported in Figures 6 and 12 and Table 6.

M1.justification: The core StepMerge and AnyOrder estimators remain, but v3 adds a substantial model-adaptation procedure: two-stage distillation-based finetuning of LLaDA using a block-respecting any-order autoregressive objective before RL (Appendix C.1.2). Its new LLaDA recipe also imposes left-to-right attention ordering within simultaneously decoded token pairs, whereas v1 permits mutual attention within a decoded group.

E1.justification: v3 adds distillation training using 150,000 Intellect-SFT prompts spanning chat, instruction following, code, science, tool use, and mathematics (Appendix C.1.2). This substantially expands the training data and task mixture. The evaluated tasks remain Sudoku, Countdown, GSM8K, MATH500, and unprompted toxicity steering; applying AnyOrder to the retained math benchmarks does not itself add task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated AnyOrder-versus-diffu-GRPO comparisons on adapted LLaDA (Figures 6 and 12); v1's AnyOrder experiments compared against DDPO and StepMerge on toxicity steering. The original StepMerge benchmark comparators—LLaDA, LLaDA 1.5, d1, and wd1—and the DDPO toxicity comparison remain.

E3.justification: The added causal-LLaDA experiments introduce validation-based checkpoint selection and a separate RL protocol, including unquantized LoRA, no prompt masking, group size 8, and two inner updates, with shared settings for AnyOrder and diffu-GRPO (Appendix C.1.2–C.1.3). These are new experimental settings, not evidence that the original StepMerge experiments changed. v3 also omits GPT2-XL generative perplexity from the reported toxicity evaluation.

E4.justification: v3 adds an ablation testing whether the initial Intellect-SFT finetuning stage improves subsequent GSM8K and MATH500 performance (Table 6). It removes the perplexity-based stability analysis and v1's immediate-EOS diagnostic observation for LLaDA. The StepMerge N sensitivity study, likelihood-discrepancy diagnostic, and AnyOrder-versus-StepMerge toxicity ablation remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. The added results retain point estimates and learning curves without uncertainty estimates. Changes to reward-standard-deviation normalization concern the training objective, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds adapted-LLaDA learning curves on GSM8K and MATH500 and Table 6 results: task-only finetuning yields 55.34% and 16.80%, versus 59.21% and 22.00% with the initial Intellect-SFT stage. These are new settings, not improvements over v1's original LLaDA results. v1 Table 2 and v3 Table 4 are numerically identical. Toxicity-score curves are redisplayed, while generative-perplexity results and the immediate-EOS finding disappear.

T1.justification: v3 removes the reasonable-policy assumption, Definition 4.2, the necessary-and-sufficient one-pass characterization in Theorem 4.3, and its Appendix A.3 proof. A constructive decoding explanation replaces this formal characterization. The policy-gradient theorem, StepMerge approximation bound, and their appendix proofs remain, so the theoretical scope is substantially narrowed.

C1.justification: The policy-gradient framework, two estimators, conditional exactness of AnyOrder, and four-benchmark state-of-the-art claims remain. v3 drops formal characterization of any-order causality as an advertised contribution and explicitly claims AnyOrder superiority over diffu-GRPO on compatible reasoning models, extending the empirical claim beyond v1's DDPO toxicity demonstration.

C2.justification: v1 hypothesizes that LLaDA relies on information stored in masked-token hidden states; v3 instead emphasizes training–inference attention mismatch and distinguishes running any-order decoding from obtaining good samples. The perplexity-based stability interpretation and the open question about large-scale RL-only versus supervised post-training disappear. Limitations now center on the absence of a strong general-purpose model supporting any-order decoding.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information: Appendix B.1 specifies the KL estimator; Appendix C supplies checkpoint identities, adaptation instructions, LoRA and quantization settings, temperatures, per-task hyperparameters, and FLOP-estimation formulas. Appendix E adds dataset and software licensing tables, and the abstract adds a project-page code-access statement. Details for retained StepMerge and Eso-LM experiments are largely newly disclosed, rather than demonstrated setting changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the adaptation pipeline, including Set Diffusion, LLaDA 2.0, dInfer, Fast-dLLM, LoRA, and dataset/software sources. GPT2 and DeepSeek-R1 references disappear with their associated discussions. Section 6 sharpens its criticism of coupled-GRPO's approximation and TraceRL's theoretical justification, while retaining the same overall positioning within diffusion-model RL.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, estimator explanations, and discussion are extensively rewritten. AnyOrder now precedes StepMerge in both methods and experiments, and an any-order autoregressive background subsection is added. Appendices are reorganized around method details, experimental recipes, additional results, and assets; the contents page and LLM-usage section disappear. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Toxicity results formerly shown in dual-axis Figures 8–9 become Tables 2–3 and appendix Figures 10–11 without perplexity axes. New reasoning curves, decoding pseudocode, and detail/asset tables are added. The bidirectional comparison panel and separate parallel-decoding illustration are removed; retained benchmark displays largely preserve their content.

improvement.justification: The added reasoning tests and detailed adaptation, hyperparameter, and FLOP recipes make AnyOrder easier to assess and reproduce, improving on v1's toxicity-only RL evaluation of that estimator. The net gain is limited: v3 removes the formal AnyOrder characterization and perplexity evidence, the new reasoning model requires additional finetuning, and its MATH500 curve fluctuates and finishes near its starting accuracy. The unchanged StepMerge results provide no same-setting performance improvement.
